title: The invisible gorilla
hook: in a study by Simons and Chabris, viewers counting basketball passes missed a person in a gorilla suit

segments.voice: Yesterday, the root of character: William James's power of bringing a wandering attention back, over and over again. Your line was bring it back. How many turns did you count? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

Count the passes. That's the whole job. On a short video, a few people in white shirts and a few in black shirts weave around each other, bouncing basketballs. Watch only the white team, and count how many times they pass the ball. Easy enough. You keep a careful tally. Partway through, a person in a full gorilla suit walks right into the middle of the game, stops, faces the camera, thumps their chest, and walks off. Afterward, the researchers ask one question: did you notice anything unusual? Close to half the people who watched it said no.
screen: `COUNT THE WHITE TEAM'S PASSES.` → `A GORILLA WALKS THROUGH.` → `DID YOU SEE ANYTHING?`

segments.voice: The psychologists Daniel Simons and Christopher Chabris ran this study, and the title of their paper was Gorillas in Our Midst. The name for what happened is inattentional blindness: when attention is fully on one task, something plainly in view can go unseen. Viewers didn't report seeing it and then forgetting. As far as they could tell, it was never there. The people who missed the gorilla weren't careless. They were doing exactly what they were asked, and doing it well. The focus that made them good counters is the same focus that hid the gorilla. Attention works like a flashlight: what it lights up gets sharper, and everything outside the beam goes darker. You can't have the beam without the dark. And there's a second, quieter lesson. From the inside, missing something doesn't feel like missing anything. Nobody watching that video felt a gap. The scene seemed complete. That's why the blind spot is so easy to live in. A person can count passes all day at work, at home, in a marriage, and walk right past something that matters, standing in the middle of the room thumping its chest. So the question that comes out of this lab isn't how do I see everything. Nobody can. It's a humbler one: what am I missing? Asked now and then, it widens the beam just enough.
screen: `GORILLAS IN OUR MIDST.` · `FOCUS HIDES WHAT IT ISN'T ON.` · `MISSING FEELS LIKE NOTHING.` · `ASK: WHAT AM I MISSING?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what you're not seeing. Settle, and breathe. First, the room. Without moving much, let your eyes find three things you hadn't noticed before: a color, a shadow, a sound underneath the other sounds. Then close your eyes and turn the question inward. Bring to mind one person you see often. Ask, gently: what about them have I been missing while I count my passes? Don't force an answer. Just hold the question open. The bell holds the time.
The invisible gorilla. Something plainly in view that goes unseen, because attention is busy somewhere else. Today's word.
Your line: what am I missing. Today, once in a meeting and once at home, pause your counting for a breath and ask it. Then look. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Researchers study inattentional blindness by giving people a demanding task, such as counting passes, and asking afterward whether they noticed an unexpected event that happened in plain view.

trapdoor: what you thought: the invisible gorilla is a trick video to catch out careless people.
what it means: attention is a beam. what it lights gets sharper, and what's outside it can go unseen, even in plain view.

what a scholar hears: inattentional blindness, studied by Simons and Chabris in Gorillas in Our Midst, where an unexpected event in the middle of the scene often went unreported by viewers busy counting.

notes: Editor: replaced 'Not glanced at and forgotten. Unseen.' (the paper measured reports, not eye fixations) with a claim about what viewers reported; cut the stock 'more than a party trick' line and the superlative 'the thing that matters most'.

'Close to half' paraphrases the paper's overall rate of viewers who failed to notice (reported near half across conditions). Confirm the figure and that it is fair for the gorilla condition described.

The hook describes the gorilla stopping, facing the camera and thumping its chest, which matches the paper's gorilla condition as commonly described; confirm. Team shirt colors and the 'count the white team' instruction: confirm.
